questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Identify the acoustic feature that organises a listener's attention
questions.stem: At a station acoustics review, a planner asks which single feature of a sound work the passing listener actually registers.

options.text: Listeners register change over time, so a sound that arrives, recurs and stops draws attention by contrast
Listeners register only the loudest passage, treating the quieter stretches of the piece as recording faults
options.misconception: believes attention rests on peak volume alone

options.text: Listeners register the position of the speaker in the hall more strongly than the order in which sounds arrive
options.misconception: assumes spatial source outranks temporal order

options.text: Listeners register the meaning of any spoken words in the piece before attending to its sound qualities
options.misconception: prioritises verbal meaning over sonic form

questions.explanation: Hearing is change-sensitive: arrival, recurrence and silence organise what we notice. Peak level is one element of that contrast, and spatial or verbal priorities are not acoustic criteria.
questions.hint: Think about what changes the ears compare over time.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of unfilled positions in a participatory work
questions.stem: A participatory concourse board offers 36 marker slots, and 24 commuters have each filled one distinct slot, leaving the rest blank.
questions.explanation: Each commuter fills one slot, so 24 of the 36 are taken and 36 minus 24 leaves 12 blank. Counting repeat placements as new ones would inflate the total and shrink the remainder wrongly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how omitting a group from a wall text shapes a visitor's reading
questions.stem: A planner is told that a gallery's wall text was edited to omit a named group, and she asks what that silence accomplishes.

answer.exemplar: An exclusion works by making a group invisible in the official account of the show. Because wall text is read as the authoritative description, an omission is taken as fact rather than as an editorial decision, so what has been left out appears never to have been present. The work itself may still hang on the wall, but the text teaches visitors how to read it and it denies the standing of the group whose presence the silence erases.

questions.explanation: Wall text carries authority, so an omission reads as fact, not editorial choice. A narrowed label that contradicts the show's own documentation exposes the exclusion by its clash.
questions.hint: Ask what the label claims by what it leaves out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data on how viewers register repetition and its interval
questions.stem: A station poster grid repeats one motif, and a survey of eight waiting commuters found that five noticed the spacing between repetitions.

options.text: The spacing proves the posters were mass printed, since hand made layouts rarely leave regular gaps
options.misconception: assumes regular spacing indicates machine printing

options.text: The spacing creates a rhythm that makes the grid read as a sequence rather than as a set of independent panels
The spacing means the repeated motif carries no meaning, because repetition always cancels a symbol's charge
options.misconception: believes repetition destroys symbol meaning

options.text: The spacing is unimportant because viewers read a poster one panel at a time and never scan the whole grid
options.misconception: assumes viewers never scan the whole composition

questions.explanation: The interval turns separate panels into a sequence a viewer can scan. A print-shop reading of regular gaps misses that rhythm, and the idea that repetition drains meaning contradicts the grid's pull.
questions.hint: Consider what the gap between repeats lets the eye do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rhetoric of the propaganda poster
questions.learningObjective: Identify the persuasive device used in a civic propaganda image

stimulus.body: A wartime civic poster shows a large upright fist lifting a torch above a row of marching figures. The palette is limited to red, black and off-white, and the torch sits on the vertical centre line. A slogan runs along the bottom in condensed capitals. The sheet was printed in bulk for public posting.

questions.stem: A planner catalogues a civic poster for a station wall and must decide which rhetorical device the designer used.

options.text: The condensed capitals at the bottom edge imitate a classified notice, keeping casual readers from stopping
options.misconception: believes the lettering is designed to repel attention

options.text: The limited red and black palette mainly hides printing costs, since fewer inks were cheaper to buy
options.misconception: reads the restricted palette as a budget decision

options.text: The raised torch and upright fist act as emblems of collective resolve, summoning a public to a single course
The row of marching figures is a documentary photograph, so the poster reports one specific real parade
options.misconception: treats a stylised image as a photograph

questions.explanation: The fist, torch, uniform figures and limited palette all work together to urge one collective response. A cost reading ignores that each element serves persuasion, and no photograph appears here.
questions.hint: Ask what the raised torch and the lifted fist are doing.

options.misconception: believes handmade posters argue for trained artists

questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many complete repetitions fit inside a timed soundscape
questions.stem: A platform soundscape repeats a 45-second motif throughout a 6-minute piece. How many complete repetitions of the motif are heard?
questions.explanation: Six minutes is 360 seconds, and 360 divided by 45 gives exactly 8. Rounding the seconds incorrectly or counting the partial remainder would produce a figure of 7 or 9 instead of the true count.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a participatory work distributes authorship to its audience
questions.stem: One agenda item asks what a participatory work actually hands over to the people who come to look at it.

answer.exemplar: A participatory work hands over a defined slot in the making of the piece, not a free role. The organiser supplies the structure, the materials and the boundary, and the viewer supplies a specific contribution that could be made differently by a different visitor. The work is therefore incomplete in the gallery and finished only by attendance, which is also why its identity shifts each time it is reopened and why photographs cannot record it fully.

questions.explanation: The transfer is bounded: the organiser provides structure and the viewer a specific contribution. That is why the piece needs its audience in the room, and why a photograph is not the work.
questions.hint: Consider what the organiser keeps and gives away.

options.text: The unlabelled works are unfinished pieces, which is why the curator withheld a description of them
options.misconception: equates missing labels with unfinished work

The figures show the label is accurate, because naming most works proves the rest were deliberately omitted
options.misconception: treats partial coverage as proof of accuracy

questions.explanation: A label is a reader's only route into meaning, so unlabelled works become uninterpretable rather than hidden. The alternatives misread a coverage gap as money, incompleteness or deliberate accuracy.
questions.hint: Consider what a visitor can understand without a text.

options.misconception: reads blank panels as evidence of separate print runs

questions.stem: A survey of 96 posters in the depot displays found 72 that repeated the same weight-shifted, hand-on-hip stance. What percentage is that?
questions.explanation: Seventy-two out of 96 is three quarters, because 96 times 0.75 equals 72. Dividing in the other order or rounding 72 into 96 wrongly gives a figure away from the true 75 per cent.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a listener retains after a sound work ends
questions.stem: A rider asks what a sound work leaves behind once its final sound has faded in the concourse.

answer.exemplar: What survives a sound work is usually the shape of its ending rather than any single sound, because memory keeps the pattern of change that the ear last tracked. A long silence, a sudden cut or a fading drone will outlive the middle of the piece in a listener's account, and the residue often changes depending on where the listener stood and what else was happening around them. The work therefore continues to operate in the listener's head after the room has gone quiet.

questions.explanation: Memory preserves the pattern of change the ear last followed, so an ending is usually what lingers. Treating the residue as a single sound or a fixed message misses that what persists is a structure.
questions.hint: Think about what the ear was doing at the end.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an unexamined pose encodes a view of the body
questions.stem: A discussion opens on why a recurring advertising pose invites the charge that women are represented as objects of view.

answer.exemplar: A pose is a sentence written with the body, and this one casts the figure as something offered to be looked at: weight thrown to one side, one hand on the hip, the body angled rather than active. Because the stance is a grammatical structure rather than a private habit, repeating it across a whole campaign reproduces the same proposition each time, and viewers are asked to read themselves into that role. The critique asks what a repeated image teaches about who looks and who is looked at.

questions.explanation: The stance is a claim, not a mood, and repetition turns it into a rule the audience learns. Reading it as personal style removes the question of who is positioned as the object of a look.
questions.hint: Ask what the body is offering to the viewer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a countercultural poster produces its images differently
questions.stem: An inquiry asks how a countercultural poster produces its images differently from the advertising it argues against.

answer.exemplar: A countercultural poster typically works by removing the conditions that make commercial images persuasive: no studio, no paid model, no glossy separation of colour, and often no professional typesetter. What replaces them is a reproducible accident, a hand-cut stencil, a mimeographed sheet or a torn collage whose errors are visible and therefore repeatable by anyone with the same materials. The image carries the proof that ordinary people can make images, which is why the method and the message cannot be separated.

questions.explanation: The method is the argument: cheap, repeatable production shows anyone can make images, so the look and the claim are one thing. A hand-made quality read as mere style misses that link.
questions.hint: Ask what the production method proves, not how it looks.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the perceptual effect of a work that ends in silence

stimulus.body: A sound work for a station concourse runs for six minutes and then stops entirely, with no closing signal or fade-out. Staff report that commuters crossing the space slow down during the final minute. A short note in the programme calls the pause the final section of the work.

questions.stem: A listening room plays a work that ends in total silence, and a planner asks what the ending does for the audience.

options.text: The silence simply ends the piece, and the slower walking is caused by commuters checking their phones
options.misconception: explains the observed change as an unrelated cause

options.text: The silence means the equipment failed, since a composed work cannot deliberately end without sound
options.misconception: reads a planned ending as an equipment fault

options.text: The silence shows the work was unfinished, because the composer never wrote a final section
options.misconception: treats an intentional silence as a missing composition

options.text: The silence extends the work by making the change from sound to nothing an event in its own right

questions.explanation: Because the ear is trained to register change, a sudden move to nothing is a strong event, which is why the room slows. Fault, incompleteness and coincidence each offer a weaker account.
questions.hint: Ask what the change from sound to silence registers as.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Connect a participatory role to the work's dependence on attendance
questions.stem: Two claims are tested: what the visitor is asked to contribute, and why the work cannot be seen whole without visitors present.

options.text: A bounded contribution comes first, and the work's completeness comes second, since one visitor finishes it
options.misconception: believes one visitor can finish the piece

options.text: A bounded contribution comes first, and the work's incompleteness comes second, since nobody supplies it
Open artistic freedom comes first, and the work's incompleteness comes second, since outcomes vary
options.misconception: confuses open-ended tasks with genuine participation

options.text: A bounded contribution comes first, and the work's incompleteness comes second, since photographs record it
options.misconception: believes documentation supplies the missing part

questions.explanation: The role is a specified act, and the work stays incomplete without the audience that performs it. Freedom without a task, one visitor finishing it, or a photograph in place of the crowd each fail it.
questions.hint: Establish the assigned task before judging completeness.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a catalogue's coverage reshapes what a show appears to contain
questions.stem: A catalogue describes a show and names only part of it, and a planner asks what the visitor therefore concludes about the whole.

options.text: The visitor suspects the unlabelled works were removed by the gallery, so the catalogue documents a censorship
options.misconception: jumps to a censorship story without evidence

options.text: The visitor correctly sees the catalogue as selective, since trained audiences read catalogues as partial
options.misconception: assumes visitors always read a catalogue as incomplete

options.text: The visitor takes the labelled works as the full exhibition, because the catalogue is trusted as complete
The visitor ignores the catalogue entirely, since most people say they read only the wall labels in a gallery
options.misconception: overstates how rarely catalogues are consulted

questions.explanation: Catalogues function as complete accounts, so their silences are read as the shape of the show. Partial reading, censorship and total avoidance each require more scepticism than the format invites.
questions.hint: Ask how a reader treats a catalogue's silence.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the length of an interval defined by a cell and a rest
questions.stem: A printed score repeats a 7-beat cell separated by a 3-beat rest. How many beats pass between the start of one cell and the start of the next?
questions.explanation: The cell occupies 7 beats and the rest adds 3 more, so 7 plus 3 gives 10 beats between starting points. Subtracting the rest from the cell would give 4, which the score does not describe.
questions.hint: Add the length of the cell and the length of the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rhetoric of the propaganda poster
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a poster's form works on the reader
questions.stem: An essay is commissioned on how a civic poster persuades, and the editor asks for the formal devices to be named.

answer.exemplar: The persuasion happens in the arrangement rather than in the slogan alone. A single dominant figure holds the centre, a limited palette removes incidental detail so nothing competes for the eye, and a strong diagonal or a raised arm substitutes for argument, converting a political programme into a direction the body can read. Type sits at the edge as a conclusion rather than a reason, and the viewer is given a posture to adopt before a single word has been taken in, which is why the sheet works at a distance and in passing.

questions.explanation: Scale, palette, direction and the placement of type do the persuading before the wording is read. Crediting only the slogan, or only the figure, misses how the composition is the argument.
questions.hint: Consider the layout before you read the words.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: Compare two poster sets using their counted production features
questions.stem: Two poster sets were counted: one run of 48 sheets showed uneven inking and hand-cut edges, while a run of 52 used flat machine colour and cut edges.

options.text: The 48-sheet run was commercial, because uneven inking is a defect that a factory press would correct
options.misconception: treats visible irregularity as a printing error

options.text: The 52-sheet run was hand produced, since the larger run shows the effort that manual work requires
options.misconception: infers hand method from the size of the run

options.text: Both runs were hand produced, because printed posters were not yet available to political groups
options.misconception: invents a technical history that was never the case

options.text: The 48-sheet run was hand produced and the 52-sheet run was printed commercially, so size tells you nothing

questions.explanation: Uneven inking and hand-cut edges identify hand production, and flat machine colour with cut edges identifies the press. The alternatives reverse the evidence or mistake irregularity for a fault.
questions.hint: Read the edges and the inking before the run size.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a photocopied poster's stance is read against the viewer's own body

stimulus.body: A photocopied poster shows a woman standing with her weight on one leg, one hand resting on her hip, shoulders angled, and her face turned slightly away from the viewer. Below the figure a single line asks readers to imagine themselves in her position. A second poster in the same series shows a figure climbing a ladder in profile.

questions.stem: A women's group photocopies a poster and analyses the model's stance, and a planner asks what the two posters together argue.

options.text: The first image is a study of balance and the second of climbing, so the pair is an exercise in posture
options.misconception: reduces the pair to a manual of body positions

options.text: The first offers a position to be looked at while the second shows a body acting, so the pair asks who looks
The first image is a fashion advertisement and the second is its rebuttal, so the pair documents a dispute
options.misconception: invents a commercial source and a dispute

options.text: The two images are interchangeable, since both show one woman in a narrow space, and the poses carry it
options.misconception: treats the difference between the two stances as negligible

questions.explanation: Set side by side, a body to be seen and a body acting make the viewer's position visible, which is the question the pair raises. Posture study, dispute and interchangeability each miss it.
questions.hint: Ask what changes when the two images are read together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Link what the ear registers to what a listener carries away
questions.stem: Two steps are needed: state what the ear registers in a sound work, then state what survives once the work has ended.

options.text: Change in sound comes first, and the printed programme comes second, which is what a listener keeps for later
options.misconception: assumes the text is the lasting object of a sound work

options.text: Volume comes first, and the loudest passage comes second, which is what a listener keeps for later
options.misconception: believes listeners retain the loudest moment

options.text: Change in sound comes first, and the remembered pattern of change comes second, which is what a listener keeps
Change in sound comes first, and nothing comes second, since a work vanishes entirely once the sound stops
options.misconception: denies any lasting effect on the listener

questions.explanation: The ear registers change, and what persists is the shape of that change rather than a single loud moment. A text, a volume peak and complete disappearance each fail to describe the residue.
questions.hint: Begin with what changes, then ask what is remembered.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Identify the decision a participatory work reserves for its organiser
questions.stem: A curator's note asks what a participatory work keeps for itself while handing the rest to the public.

options.text: It keeps the exhibition fee, so the visitor supplies the material and the organiser supplies the money
options.misconception: confuses the economic arrangement with the artistic one

options.text: It keeps nothing at all, since a fully open work is one in which every decision is made by the audience
options.misconception: believes participation means the absence of any structure

options.text: It keeps the finished result, so the audience contributes only effort while the organiser holds the outcome
options.misconception: treats audience work as labour without authorship

options.text: It keeps the frame, the materials and the rules, leaving the content of contributions to the visitor

questions.explanation: The organiser supplies the frame and the rules; the content of the contribution is what the visitor adds. Total openness, a held-back result and a payment arrangement each misplace the authorship.
questions.hint: Ask who decides the rules of the task.

questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of works in a show that carry no label
questions.stem: A travelling show hangs 31 works in total, and its printed label names 24 of them. How many works carry no label at all?
questions.explanation: The unlabelled works are those not named, so 31 minus 24 leaves 7. Subtracting in the other direction would give a negative number, and reading 31 as the labelled count would inflate the answer to 55.
questions.hint: Take the total away from the number that are named.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Explain how repetition and its gap work together in a composition
questions.stem: A talk is asked to explain why a repeated element and the gap between its appearances must be considered together.

answer.exemplar: Repetition supplies the element and the interval supplies the metre, and a composition is made by the pair rather than by either alone. A short gap after a strong mark produces urgency and an expectation of return; a long gap produces a rest that the returning element then seems to interrupt. Because the ear measures expectation against arrival, the interval governs how much weight the repetition carries, which is why a work that changes only the spacing of an unchanged figure can sound entirely different from one that changes the figure.

questions.explanation: The ear measures expectation against arrival, so the gap governs how much weight the repeated element carries. Treating repetition as the whole effect, or the gap as emptiness, misses the joint work.
questions.hint: Ask how long the ear waits before the element returns.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rhetoric of the propaganda poster
questions.learningObjective: Interpret archive counts of a repeated emblem in civic posters
questions.stem: An archive coding found 55 of 120 civic posters used a single raised-arm emblem, and among those 55, 41 placed the arm in the upper third of the sheet.

options.text: The emblem recurs widely but sits high on the sheet, so the posters were hung from a single standard rail
options.misconception: infers a mounting arrangement from image placement

options.text: The emblem recurs widely and sits high on the sheet, so it gains both reach and visual priority
Only 41 posters were emblematic, and the other 79 simply have not yet been catalogued by the archive
options.misconception: invents a cataloguing backlog to explain the count

options.text: The emblem is too common to carry meaning, since a device in nearly half of posters cannot persuade
options.misconception: equates frequency with the absence of persuasive force

questions.explanation: Frequent recurrence gives an emblem shared recognition, and high placement gives it priority in view. A mounting habit, a cataloguing gap and a mechanical reading of frequency each misread it.
questions.hint: Read the reach of the device and its position separately.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a hand-stencilled poster's forms and their stated aim

stimulus.body: A hand-stencilled poster shows a simple open hand printed in one colour on rough paper, with cut edges visible along every edge of the shape. The only text, applied with a brush, reads: this is yours to copy. The sheet is the first of a set of 30 identical stencils left in a depot hallway for anyone to take and use.

questions.stem: A hand-stencilled poster is pinned to a noticeboard at the depot, and a planner asks what the sheet is asking of its reader.

options.text: The stencil and its invitation ask the reader to buy the remaining sheets, making the work a small sale
options.misconception: treats a free stencil as a sales offer

options.text: The stencil and its invitation ask the reader to keep the sheet up, making the work a record of an event
options.misconception: reads the copy instruction as an instruction to display

options.text: The stencil and its invitation ask the reader to reproduce the image, making the work a tool not an object
The stencil and its invitation ask the reader to judge the brush lettering, making the work a lettering lesson
options.misconception: reduces the poster to a craft demonstration

questions.explanation: A stencil that is given away, with wording that says so, makes the image a reproducible instrument. Displaying, buying and craft instruction each misread what the sheet hands to the reader.
questions.hint: Ask what a giveaway stencil permits the reader to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: Sequence an observation about a pose into the claim it supports
questions.stem: The board must do two things: describe what the recurring pose positions the body to do, then state the claim that follows.

options.text: The body is positioned to move, and the claim follows that the advertisement celebrates athletic training
options.misconception: reads a static pose as evidence of sport

options.text: The body is positioned to be viewed, and the claim follows that the audience is addressed as the looked-at
options.misconception: reverses who occupies the position of object

options.text: The body is positioned to work, and the claim follows that the advertisement celebrates industrial labour
options.misconception: reads a display pose as a reference to work

options.text: The body is positioned to be viewed, and the claim follows that the audience is addressed as the one looking

questions.explanation: A pose that displays the body to a viewer places the viewer as observer, and that is the claim repetition makes. Reversed roles, industrial labour and athletic training each contradict it.
questions.hint: Decide who is looking before deciding who is looked at.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Identify the perceptual difference between a first and a repeated sound
questions.stem: A listening study asks what the ear registers when a sound that has already occurred returns for a second time.

options.text: The return is heard as a brand new event, because the ear has no memory of the sound that came before
options.misconception: believes hearing has no memory at all

options.text: The return is measured against the first occurrence, so repetition is heard as a comparison between two events
The return is heard only as a change in volume, since pitch and timbre are irrelevant to repetition
options.misconception: reduces repetition to a level difference

options.text: The return is heard only as a change in position, since the ear cannot judge an event without knowing the room
options.misconception: reduces repetition to a spatial difference

questions.explanation: A return is always heard against what preceded it, so repetition is a comparison between two events. A memoryless ear, a level-only reading and a spatial-only reading each deny it.
questions.hint: Think about what the second occurrence is measured against.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of rows in a participatory formation
questions.stem: A participatory score asks 24 commuters to stand in rows of four, with every row completely filled. How many rows are formed?
questions.explanation: Twenty-four commuters in groups of four give exactly 6 rows, since 4 times 6 is 24. Dividing the other way round, or rounding up for a partial row, would not match the condition.
questions.hint: Divide the number of people by the size of a row.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how editing a wall text can change a work's meaning
questions.stem: A short note is requested on why editing the wall text of a stable work can change what that work appears to be.

answer.exemplar: A wall text is the frame through which a visitor reads a work, so editing it can change the work's apparent content without touching the work at all. Remove the line recording the community from which the materials were gathered and the pieces become a private formal experiment; keep the line and they become a record of collective effort. The objects stay identical and are not innocent of meaning, but the text tells the visitor which reading to adopt, which is why a modest change of wording can carry a large interpretive consequence.

questions.explanation: The work stays put while the frame that directs its reading changes, so a small edit can redirect interpretation. The objects are not meaningless, but the text tells visitors which account to adopt.
questions.hint: Ask what the text tells a visitor to read the objects as.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the structure of a grid built on a fixed repeating interval
questions.stem: In a grid of 40 posters, the repeated mark falls on every 5th panel, and a short survey records that viewers took longer to find the mark in the second half of the sheet.

options.text: The 5-panel interval was chosen at random, since survey times were recorded to test the survey itself
options.misconception: invents a testing procedure to explain the design

options.text: The fixed 5-panel interval organises the sheet, and the longer search shows the pattern weakens as it repeats
options.misconception: reads search time as a decline in the pattern's force

options.text: The fixed 5-panel interval organises the sheet, and the longer search shows a regular pattern is hard to read
The longer search shows the grid is badly designed, since any repeating pattern should be found at once
options.misconception: treats ordinary search effort as a design fault

questions.explanation: A repeated element every fifth panel does impose order, and the slowing search shows regularity does not make a mark immediate. Declining force, a random choice and a design fault each misread it.
questions.hint: Separate the grid from the effort of finding the mark.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rhetoric of the propaganda poster
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a propaganda poster's typography as a rhetorical device

stimulus.body: A civic poster carries a single line of condensed capitals running the full width of the sheet near the bottom. The type is tight, heavy and evenly spaced, with no italic, no lower case and no decorative flourish. Above the line sits a raised fist in flat red. The paper is thin enough to show the grain of the wall behind it.

questions.stem: A poster shown at the depot carries a slogan in capitals, and a planner asks what the typography itself contributes.

options.text: The tight capitals are chosen so the line is unreadable at a distance, keeping the emblem as the only message
options.misconception: mistakes a legible slogan for an unreadable one

options.text: The tight capitals mark the line as a quotation from an earlier text, so the poster borrows an older authority
options.misconception: reads letterform as evidence of quotation

options.text: The tight capitals show the sheet was produced cheaply, since mixed case would have needed a second type block
options.misconception: derives production method from the letterforms

options.text: The tight capitals give the line the force of a statement to be shouted, which supports the emblem above it

questions.explanation: Heavy, tight capitals read as emphatic declaration and lift the emblem into a slogan. Quotation, cheap production and illegibility each mistake a stylistic choice for a fact about the sheet.
questions.hint: Consider how the letterforms would be read aloud.

questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: Sequence production evidence into the political claim a poster makes
questions.stem: The panel is asked to settle two things about a protest sheet: what shows it was made by hand, and what that production choice argues.

options.text: Hand-cut edges show hand making, and the argument is that only professional skills give a valid image
options.misconception: inverts self-production into a claim for expertise

options.text: Hand-cut edges show hand making, and the argument is that ordinary people can produce their own images
A flat machine colour shows hand making, and the argument is that ordinary people should print more posters
options.misconception: misreads machine printing as hand work and misstates it

options.text: Hand-cut edges show hand making, and the argument is that the poster should be collected rather than used
options.misconception: recasts a working sheet as a collector's item

questions.explanation: Visible hand cutting is the evidence, and the claim that anyone can make images is what it is for. Expertise, machine colour and collector status each contradict the evidence or the message.
questions.hint: Name the physical trace, then the claim it carries.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a repeated pose teaches a viewer about bodies
questions.stem: A seminar asks what a repeated pose teaches the people who see it, and the discussion turns to the viewer's own body.

options.text: It teaches only an ideal of beauty, because posture carries no social meaning beyond appearance
options.misconception: reduces the pose to aesthetics alone

options.text: It teaches nothing at all, because a pose in an image has no effect on the behaviour of those who see it

It teaches resistance, because any repeated image is a target that viewers learn to question

questions.explanation: Repetition is instruction: a stance shown again and again is a template the viewer can copy, so the image teaches behaviour. Neutrality, beauty and automatic resistance each understate that.
questions.hint: Ask what the viewer is invited to do with their own body.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Explain why visitors accept a specified task in a participatory work
questions.stem: A reflective note is asked for on why visitors accept a bounded task rather than a licence to make the work themselves.

answer.exemplar: Visitors accept a bounded task because a defined contribution is legible in a way that open freedom is not. When a sheet asks for one word, a mark or a position, a person can judge in a second whether they have done it correctly, and the pleasure comes precisely from that clear completion. Open invitation inverts the balance, since the visitor must first invent a task and then worry whether the result is any good. The structure is not a limitation on the audience but the thing that makes participation possible in a public place with a queue behind it.

questions.explanation: A clear, quickly completable task makes joining possible in public; open freedom adds a second problem first. The structure is not a limit on the audience but the condition of participation.
questions.hint: Ask how quickly a visitor can tell they have done the task.

options.text: The unlabelled room loses most of the traffic, so a missing text measurably reduces how far a visitor travels

questions.explanation: Only about a third of those who stopped at the labelled section went on to the far room, so the missing text plausibly cost them the journey. Content, success and reading speed each misattribute it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Read a repeated element through the length of the interval in a wall text

stimulus.body: A wall text describes a woven hanging: the same banded pattern appears eleven times from top to bottom, and between each band the weaver left a plain strip of exactly the same width as the band itself. The final band at the bottom is followed by a longer plain strip that runs to the edge of the cloth. A note beside the case records that the maker counted the bands while weaving.

questions.stem: A wall text describes a hanging whose banded pattern repeats at a measured interval, and a planner asks what the interval contributes.

options.text: The equal alternation of band and plain strip shows the cloth was machine woven to a fixed repeat setting
options.misconception: reads a measured repeat as evidence of machine weaving

options.text: Equal alternation of band and plain strip sets a countable unit, so the pattern reads as measured repetition
Equal alternation of band and plain strip hides the pattern, since contrast of this strength defeats the eye
options.misconception: claims strong contrast makes a pattern invisible

options.text: The equal alternation of band and plain strip is decorative only, and the maker's count shows numbered bands
options.misconception: reads the maker's count as numbered bands

questions.explanation: A regular alternation of equal units lets the pattern be counted, and countability makes the repetition legible as order. Machine weaving, hidden pattern and numbered bands each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the unit could be counted, and what that allows.

questions.stem: Two things are at issue in a civic poster: which device carries the message, and what response that device is built to produce.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: Compare a countercultural poster and a commercial poster by their means of production
questions.stem: A panel discussion asks what distinguishes a countercultural poster from a commercial poster in the methods that produce their images.

options.text: The countercultural sheet is printed in greyscale, because colour printing was unavailable to political groups
options.misconception: invents a technical constraint to explain the look

options.text: The countercultural sheet is more expensive to produce, which signals the seriousness of the cause it supports
options.misconception: assumes cost indicates the depth of a message

options.text: The countercultural sheet is unsigned, since anonymity is always the mark of a collective political voice
options.misconception: treats anonymity as the sign of a collective message

options.text: The countercultural sheet is reproducible by its readers, so its production method is part of its argument

questions.explanation: The sheet's method is reproducible and visible, and the argument sits inside that reproducibility. Cost, anonymity and greyscale each substitute a superficial feature for the real link.
questions.hint: Ask what the production method makes possible for readers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many models were replaced in a poster series
questions.stem: A workshop replaced one in every four posed models among the 120 models shown, replacing each with a model in an active stance. How many models were replaced?
questions.explanation: One in four of 120 models is 120 divided by 4, which is 30 models. Reading the fraction as one in forty, or applying it to the replacements, gives a different and wrong count.
questions.hint: Divide the models by the denominator of the fraction.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sound work's ending often dominates the listener's account
questions.stem: A note is requested on why the ending of a sound work so often dominates the listener's account of it.

answer.exemplar: The ending dominates because the ear is alert to change and the close of a piece is the largest change it is asked to process. A sound that stops, fades or cuts arrives after minutes of continuous expectation, and that contrast is registered as a boundary marking the work's end rather than as one more event within it. Because listeners tend to recount a piece from the point where it changed most sharply, the final gesture colours the memory of everything that preceded it, which is why the last section of a work is often the part people describe with the greatest certainty.

questions.explanation: The ending is the largest change the ear must process, marking a boundary rather than another event, so it colours the memory. Treating it as ordinary misses how contrast shapes listening.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of change the close of a piece represents.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: Interpret rider feedback showing which participatory invitation was taken up
questions.stem: Rider feedback shows 41 of 66 chose to add a mark at the shared board, while only 12 of 66 added a written comment to the comment slot beside it.

options.text: The mark was taken up because riders were trained by staff to use the board, so the instructions decided it
options.misconception: invents staff training the data does not mention

options.text: The mark was taken up because it takes seconds, while the comment asked for writing and a personal position
The comment slot failed because the board was placed in a dead corner, not on the main route
options.misconception: invents a location problem the feedback never records

options.text: The figures show riders prefer images over words in general, which says nothing about the board's design
options.misconception: over-generalises a design-specific result

questions.explanation: The two invitations differ in cost: a mark is quick, a comment requires writing and a view. Staff training, a bad location and a general preference for images each go beyond what the figures record.
questions.hint: Compare what each invitation asked the rider to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a single quoted line as evidence of a label's exclusions

stimulus.body: A gallery guide quotes one sentence from a wall text: this series of 24 works was assembled over ten years from printed matter that the makers collected daily. The guide then notes that the catalogue records that the series was made collectively by nine people, and that the wall text does not say so. A second wall text in the same room names the nine.

questions.stem: A gallery guide quotes one sentence of wall text and leaves the rest out, and a planner asks what the omission conceals.

options.text: It conceals the material used, so the quoted sentence makes the series sound more precious than it is
options.misconception: misdirects the omission onto the value of the materials

options.text: It conceals the date of the work, so the quoted sentence gives no sense of how long the series took
options.misconception: reads the omission as a missing date, not a missing author

options.text: It conceals that the series was made collectively, so quoting the sentence supports a solitary authorship
It conceals nothing, because the second wall text in the same room names the nine makers for anyone to read
options.misconception: treats a nearby text as cancelling the omission

questions.explanation: The quoted sentence leaves out the collective authorship, so it supports a solitary maker the catalogue contradicts. A nearby naming text helps only the reader who walks on and asks.
questions.hint: Ask what the quoted line makes true on its own.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: Determine the interval and its effect in a repeated composition
questions.stem: A further note asks the board to settle two matters about a repeated composition: how long the interval is, and what it produces for the reader.

options.text: The interval is a fixed number of units, and it produces no effect, since repetition leaves a reader unmoved
options.misconception: denies any effect of a repeated structure

options.text: The interval is a fixed number of units, and it produces a sense of irregularity that keeps the reader alert
options.misconception: confuses a regular interval with an irregular one

options.text: The interval is unpredictable, and it produces a counted pulse the reader can follow across the work
options.misconception: keeps the effect but denies the interval is fixed

options.text: The interval is a fixed number of units, and it produces a counted pulse the reader can follow across the work

questions.explanation: A fixed interval is countable, and countability is what gives a reader a pulse to follow. Irregularity, an unpredictable gap and complete inertness each contradict the stated regularity or its effect.
questions.hint: Settle the length of the gap before judging its effect.
